title: How to Price a Product in 2026 (+ Pricing Calculator) - Shopify

facts.fact: Shopify's page states that the easiest way to price a product is to add up all costs involved in bringing it to market and then add a markup on top.
facts.quote: The easiest way to price a product is to add up all the costs involved in bringing it to market, then add a markup on top.

facts.fact: According to New York University data cited by Shopify, the average gross profit margin for general retail is 33.18%.
facts.quote: General retail: 33.18%

facts.fact: According to New York University data cited by Shopify, the average gross profit margin for furniture and home furnishings is 30.28%.
facts.quote: Furniture and home furnishings: 30.28%

facts.fact: According to New York University data cited by Shopify, the average gross profit margin for electronics is 38.77%.
facts.quote: Electronics: 38.77%

facts.fact: According to New York University data cited by Shopify, the average gross profit margin for apparel is 56.88%.
facts.quote: Apparel: 56.88%

facts.fact: According to New York University data cited by Shopify, the average gross profit margin for food and grocery is 26.31%.
facts.quote: Food and grocery: 26.31%

facts.fact: Shopify's formula for cost per unit is (total variable costs + total fixed costs) divided by the number of units produced.
facts.quote: (Total variable costs + Total fixed costs) / Number of units produced = Cost per unit

facts.fact: Shopify's target price formula is cost per unit divided by (1 minus desired profit margin as a decimal).
facts.quote: Target price = (Cost per unit) / (1 - Desired profit margin as a decimal)

facts.fact: In Shopify's worked example, a desired profit margin of 20% means dividing cost per unit by 0.8.
facts.quote: if your desired profit margin is 20%, you’d divide your cost per unit by 0.8 (since 1 - 0.2 = 0.8).

facts.fact: Using the formula selling price = cost / (1 - margin), a $14.28 cost per unit at a 20% desired profit margin gives a selling price of $17.85.

facts.fact: Average selling price is calculated by dividing total revenue by the number of units sold; the page's example of 200 units sold for $5,000 yields $25.
facts.quote: So if you sold 200 units last month and brought in $5,000, your average selling price is $25.

facts.fact: In Shopify's profit margin calculator example, a $25 sale price yields a $5 profit and a 20% gross margin.
facts.quote: In the example below, a $25 sale price yields a $5 profit and a 20% gross margin.

facts.fact: In the cost-plus pricing example, a custom jewelry maker adds a 50% markup to the total cost of materials and labor to set the retail price.
facts.quote: Then, they’d add a 50% markup to arrive at the final retail price.

facts.fact: In the calculator example, an item costing $20 with a 25% markup generates a target selling price automatically.
facts.quote: if your item costs $20 to produce and you want to apply a 25% markup, the calculator will generate your target selling price automatically.

facts.fact: The page lists six common pricing strategies: cost-plus, competitive, value-based, premium, penetration, and price skimming.
facts.quote: Six common pricing strategies are cost-plus, competitive, value-based, premium, penetration, and price skimming

facts.fact: The article suggests testing a price increase of 5% to 10% on a group of SKUs and watching how sales volume responds.
facts.quote: Pick a group of SKUs and try a 5% to 10% increase.

facts.fact: Classic psychological pricing tactics include ending prices in .99 or using odd numbers to make prices feel lower.
facts.quote: Classic tactics include ending prices in .99 or using odd numbers to make prices feel lower.

facts.fact: The article recommends adding a quarterly pricing check to your calendar to avoid competitors quietly undercutting your prices.
facts.quote: add a quarterly pricing check to your calendar

facts.fact: The article recommends reviewing your costs every few months and adjusting pricing when needed.
facts.quote: Make it a habit to review your costs every few months and adjust pricing when needed.

facts.fact: The article states that a 30% markup is not the same as a 30% margin, and that confusing the two can significantly lower profit per sale.
facts.quote: A 30% markup is _not_ the same as a 30% margin, and using the wrong one can significantly lower your profit per sale.

facts.fact: Discount pricing, or placing products on sale, can encourage purchases and help clear out older inventory, but discounting too many products can make a premium brand look like a bargain retailer.
facts.quote: or placing your products on sale, can encourage purchases because shoppers feel like they’re getting a good deal.

facts.fact: The page states that a typical retail price for a product costing $10 to produce is around $14.95, based on an average retail margin of around 33%.
facts.quote: A typical retail price for a product that costs $10 to produce is around $14.95, based on an average retail margin of around 33%.

facts.fact: The page cites an average retail margin of around 33%, linking to NYU Stern (Damodaran) margin data as the source.
facts.quote: The average for retail is around [33%](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/margin.html)

facts.fact: The page recommends building price reviews into business operations on a quarterly basis to catch cost changes, competitor movements, and demand shifts.
facts.quote: Build regular price reviews into your business operations. Quarterly reviews help you catch cost changes, competitor movements, and demand shifts before they erode margins.

facts.fact: The page defines elastic demand as demand where customers are highly price-sensitive, so small price increases cause noticeable sales drops, while inelastic demand is where customers buy regardless of modest price changes.
facts.quote: Some products have “elastic” demand, where customers are highly price-sensitive and small increases cause noticeable sales drops. Others have inelastic demand, where customers will buy regardless of modest price changes.
